2. **Track it as a hypothesis** — the `hypothesis-tracking` skill can record this baptism as a candidate for Patrick while the question stays open.
3. **Reject the record** — if you believe this baptism is not Patrick's, that decision is yours to record.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

The informant was a son-in-law, making this secondary information on the birth.

Both links are rated **probable** (same_person score of 0.24, reflecting thin tree data rather than a core conflict). Facts were materialized onto I1.

One follow-up note: the relationship assertion (a_013, "Father: Thomas Flynn") was not linked — that parentage link to Thomas Flynn (I2) can be handled separately if needed.

items.weighing_analysis: The census records are contemporary recordings made near the time of Patrick's birth, while the death certificate was created 63 years later. The census informant was likely a household member with firsthand knowledge (primary or indeterminate), while the death certificate informant (son-in-law) is clearly secondary for birth facts. Two contemporary sources outweigh one later recollection by a secondary informant.

**22 person_evidence entries (pe_001 – pe_022)** were created linking the household across both census records to the five tree persons:

| Person | 1870 (src_001) | 1880 (src_002) |
|---|---|---|

Policy caps the confidence at *probable* until that gap is bridged.

James (b. ~1852) and Ellen (b. ~1855) appear in the 1870 census but are **absent from the 1880 household**. The tree records no death for either. Possible explanations:

- They were enumerated elsewhere (married, employed away, etc.)
- They left the household for another reason

This question remains open for the researcher to resolve.

agent_returns.text:
Linked the William Weller household in both census records to the tree family. Every link is `probable`, not `confident`, because the move from Horsham, Sussex to Maury County, Tennessee is unexplained.

**Links created (22 `pe_` entries, pe_001 to pe_022; pe_015 was re-worded once):**

| Person | 1870 (src_001) | 1880 (src_002) |
|---|---|---|
| I1 William Weller | pe_001–003 | pe_012–013, pe_018 |
| I2 Mary Weller | pe_004–005 | pe_014–015 |
| I3 James Weller | pe_006–007 | none |
| I4 Ellen Weller | pe_008–009 | none |
| I5 George Weller | pe_010–011 | pe_016–017 |

The wife and son relationship assertions in 1880 (a_019, a_020) also link to William as the second party (pe_015, pe_019's sibling entries, pe_020 and pe_022 cover the focus-side links). Every link scored 0.78 from `same_person`, and that score is disclosed in each rationale.

**Why probable:** Name, sex, age and birthplace agree for all five people, and the household matches the tree's parent-child edges. The 1861 tree residence is Horsham, England, and the census places are in Maury County, Tennessee, about 6,804 km away. The Tennessee wiki page names no arrival from England, and the project holds no passenger list or naturalization record that bridges the move. Under the policy that caps the link at `probable`.

**Identity question for the researcher:** In 1880 the tree children James (b. ~1852) and Ellen (b. ~1855) are absent from the household, and the tree shows no death for either. They may have died, been enumerated elsewhere, or left the household. This is not resolved by these links.

**Not done:** No new family edges were written because the tree already holds the Couple and ParentChild edges for this family. Facts from both censuses were written onto the five people (materialize_facts). `person_warnings` reports one "nonstandard place" note per person. It comes from the existing 1851 and 1861 Horsham residence facts, not from this work.

---

Linked William, Mary and George Weller in both census records as the same people already in the tree, each at "probably" because the move from Horsham, England to Tennessee is not explained by anything on file. James and Ellen, the other two children, do not appear in the 1880 household and there is no death on file for either, so their absence needs an explanation.

Next, please tell me whether James and Ellen died, were counted elsewhere, or left the household, so that the question about the family can be settled.

dimensions.rationale: All 22 person_evidence entries are factually correct. Names, ages, birthplaces, and relationships match the tree and census records. All match_scores (0.78) are accurate from same_person calls. Facts were correctly materialized onto existing tree persons. No fabricated material or unsupported claims.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: All 20 assertions from both census records (src_001 and src_002) were linked to appropriate tree persons. Five tree persons (I1–I5) received person_evidence entries covering names, births, residences, and relationships. The 1870 household (11 assertions) and 1880 household (9 assertions) were fully processed. The absence of James and Ellen from the 1880 census was flagged as an identity question. No assertions were silently omitted.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All MCP tool calls passed correct arguments. same_person calls used correct assertionId and treePersonId pairs; recordRole was correctly omitted for the assertion's own party (e.g., pe_001 for a_001 linking William to I1) and correctly supplied for the second party of relationship assertions (e.g., recordRole 'head' for a_019 linking Mary to I1). place_search and place_distance calls used semantically correct place names. wiki_read called the correct Tennessee emigration page. research_append and materialize_facts calls were well-formed. No fixture_not_found errors.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: All 22 links are scored 'probable', which is correct per the decided rule. The geographic gap (Horsham, Sussex to Maury County, Tennessee, 6804 km, with no documentary bridge or corridor) caps the link at probable, never confident. Name, age, birthplace, and household relationships all agree strongly, but the unexplained transatlantic move prevents confident. No links are speculative (which would over-apply the rule), and no links are confident (which would violate the cap). The rationales consistently name the geographic gap and distance.

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: Each rationale cites specific matching attributes: name, age, birthplace, household position, and parent-child/spouse relationships. The geographic gap is explicitly named in every rationale (e.g., 'outside 6804 km; no corridor on the Tennessee wiki page and no project bridge: nothing'). The rationales explain why the move is unexplained and why it caps confidence. Competing candidates are implicitly ruled out by the strong household and family agreement. Rationales are substantive, not generic.

dimensions.rationale: Relationship assertions in the 1880 census (a_019 wife, a_020 son) are linked on both sides. a_019 links to I1 (pe_015, pe_019) and I2 (pe_019 as focus). a_020 links to I1 (pe_016, pe_022) and I5 (pe_022 as focus). The 1870 household relationships are implicit in the household structure and are correctly linked to all five persons. Every relationship-implying assertion has person_evidence entries for both parties.

dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges
dimensions.rationale: No new persons were minted; all five census personas matched existing tree persons (I1–I5). materialize_facts was called correctly for all eight record-person pairs (5 from 1870, 3 from 1880), enriching existing persons with sourced facts (names, births, residences). No edges were written because the tree already held all necessary Couple and ParentChild relationships. The skill correctly recognized this and did not redundantly add edges. Facts were materialized with proper source references (S10, S11).

dimensions.name: Score discipline
dimensions.rationale: same_person was called for every assertion with a tree candidate: 10 calls total (one per distinct record persona and tree person pair). Each call correctly compared the record party to the tree person. For relationship assertions (a_019, a_020), recordRole was supplied to score the second party (the head). The score (0.78) was disclosed in every rationale and correctly informed confidence without overriding it: the high score did not push the link to confident despite the geographic gap. Correlation and score worked together appropriately.

output.text_response:
The person-evidence agent did **not** link assertion a_002. Here is its finding:

**Candidate reviewed:** I1 Patrick Flynn (male, born ~1845, Ireland, son of Thomas Flynn and Mary Flynn) — the only Patrick Flynn in the tree.

**Why it was not linked:** A direct contradiction blocks the link. The baptism record (src_002) gives Patrick's birthplace as **Trier, Rhine Province, Germany** (assertion a_005), while the tree records **Ireland** for I1. That birthplace conflict is unresolved — there is no `conflicts` entry covering a_002 or a_005 — so the threshold policy requires no link.

A name match alone is not identification, so the record stays unattached.

**Recommended next steps:**
1. **Conflict-resolution** — adjudicate the Germany vs. Ireland birthplace contradiction before any link can be made.
2. **Hypothesis-tracking** — optionally hold the identity as an open question while the conflict is pending.

Nothing was written to the project files; the researcher must decide how to proceed with the birthplace discrepancy.

agent_returns.text:
I did not link a_002. The record's birthplace conflicts with the tree person it would attach to, and no resolved conflict settles it, so the threshold policy calls for no link.

- **Candidate:** I1 Patrick Flynn, the only Patrick Flynn in the tree (male, birth about 1845, Ireland, son of Thomas Flynn and Mary Flynn).
- **Conflict:** The baptism record (src_002, Patrick Flynn baptism, FamilySearch ark CFLT-9K2) gives the birthplace as Trier, Rhine Province, Germany (a_005). The tree attests Ireland for I1 (F1). The source's own notes flag the same conflict against every census record for this subject.
- **Conflict register:** No `conflicts` entry covers a_002 or a_005, so the contradiction is unresolved.
- **Score:** I did not run `same_person`. A birthplace contradiction is a no-link on its own, and a score cannot promote it.
- **Nothing written:** No `person_evidence` entry, no materialized facts, and no rejection record. Only the researcher can record a rejection.

The baptism's name ("Patrick Flynn") is the only point of agreement, and a name match alone is not identification. If the researcher believes this is the same Patrick, the birthplace conflict needs adjudicating first, through conflict-resolution. Hypothesis-tracking could hold the identity as an open question in the meantime.

---
The record that names this Patrick Flynn gives his birthplace as Germany, while the family's tree entry says Ireland, and nothing on file settles which is right. Because of that, the record is not attached to the Patrick in the tree. The next step is to resolve the birthplace conflict before deciding whether this baptism belongs to him.
